736.title: the lac house
736.hook: the brothers know the house will burn, and decide to stay in it, while a digger works beneath the floor
736.howItsDone: In tellings of the Mahabharata, the brothers' patience at Varanavata is told as the fruit of Yudhishthira's calm judgment.

segments.voice: Yesterday in the lac house, Vidura's riddle, and Yudhishthira catching the smell of fat and lac — this house is made to burn. Did you hear a warning inside an ordinary sentence? Day seven hundred thirty-six.

Bhima's answer is the obvious one. If this house is made to burn, he says, let's get out of it. Let's go back to where we were safe. It's the answer that comes first, standing in a room that smells of fuel. The walls look solid. The rooms are fine and well furnished. Purochana is all smiles. And somewhere in the plaster is enough to turn the whole place into a torch. And Yudhishthira says no. We stay. Today the lac house turns into a test, not of strength, but of nerve.
screen: `BHIMA: LET'S GET OUT.` → `YUDHISHTHIRA: WE STAY.` → `A TEST OF NERVE.`

segments.voice: Yudhishthira lays out his reasons. If we run, Purochana will know we've guessed, and he'll set the fire at once, or Duryodhana's people will hunt us down. We have no allies out here, no treasury, no army. So we'll live here as if we suspect nothing. We'll go hunting in the forests, and learn every road and path. And we'll make a way out that nobody can see. Then help arrives. A man comes to them, a skilled digger, sent by Vidura. He proves who he is by repeating words that only Yudhishthira heard on the road: the riddle. And he gets to work. Under the house, from the middle of it, he digs a passage leading out, and he covers the opening so it's level with the floor. All this while, Purochana keeps watch at the door, sure that his guests know nothing. Look where the brothers' safety comes from. It doesn't come from a battle, or a god, or a miracle. It comes from patience, from paying attention, and from an uncle who sent a quiet helper. Remember the riddle: a fire that burns a whole forest can't reach the creatures that live in holes underground. Now the brothers are making their hole. They eat in the house, sleep in the house, smile at Purochana, and wait, the text says, a long time, with weapons close at hand. A house built to look kind is now answered by guests who look calm. Tomorrow, the night comes.
screen: `IF WE RUN, HE BURNS IT NOW.` · `LIVE AS IF WE SUSPECT NOTHING.` · `VIDURA'S DIGGER PROVES HIMSELF.` · `A PASSAGE UNDER THE FLOOR.` · then, large: `CALM GUESTS IN A HOUSE BUILT TO BURN.`

segments.voice: Sit steady for two minutes. Let the breath go low and slow. Choose something you're waiting through right now, a situation you can't simply walk out of. Instead of planning, for these two minutes just notice: what do you know about it, and what's quietly being prepared, by you or by someone helping? Let the body be calm while the mind stays awake. The bell holds the time.
The lac house. The brothers stay, calm on the surface, while Vidura's digger cuts a hidden passage under the floor.
Your line: the lac house. Today, when you can't leave a hard situation, quietly prepare your way out instead of panicking. Day seven hundred thirty-six.

737.title: the lac house
737.hook: a feast, a family of strangers asleep, and a fire lit from the inside
737.carry: a woman and five sons, unnamed
737.howItsDone: Some Hindus read the Mahabharata straight through over months, a section at a time, as this serial does; others meet episodes like the lac house through storytelling, theater and television.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the lac house: the brothers staying calm on the surface while a passage was dug under the floor. Did you quietly prepare a way out of something? Day seven hundred thirty-seven.

The house at Varanavata was made to look like a gift and to burn like a torch, with lac and resin and ghee worked into its walls, the text says. Under its floor there's a secret of a different kind: a tunnel, dug by a miner Vidura sent, its mouth hidden inside the house. Kunti and her sons have been living on top of a fire that hasn't been lit yet. Purochana, the man who built it, is living there too, waiting for his moment. Tonight, someone else strikes first.
screen: `A HOUSE MADE TO BURN.` → `A TUNNEL UNDER THE FLOOR.` → `TONIGHT.`

segments.voice: Kunti gives a feast. Brahmins come and eat, and women come, and when it's over, the guests go home. But a Nishada woman, a woman of the forest people, has come looking for food with her five sons. They eat and drink, and they fall asleep in the house, so heavily, the text says, they're like the dead. Then, in the dark, Bhima gets up. He sets fire first to the place where Purochana is sleeping. Then to the door. Then all around the house. And the family goes down into the tunnel, and out. In the morning the townspeople stand at the ashes, grieving. They find Purochana, burned in his own trap. And they find a woman and five young men, and they say: Kunti and her sons are dead. That's the escape. Now stay with one detail. The plan works because strangers were in the house. The text tells it quickly, and doesn't stop for them. Some readers take it plainly: fate put those bodies there, and the story needed the world to believe. Some say the poem is letting us see the cost of the cousins' quarrel, beginning with people who had no part in it. Some notice that the woman and her sons are never named, and that the silence is itself worth hearing. Here the poem doesn't pause to rule on the act. It shows it, and leaves room. The lac house was built to kill the Pandavas. It ends up killing the man who built it, and six people nobody planned for.
screen: `A FEAST, AND GUESTS WHO STAY.` · `BHIMA LIGHTS THE FIRE.` · `SIX BODIES IN THE ASHES.` · then, large: `THE ONES WITH NO NAMES.`

segments.voice: There's a cost in this story, so take it slowly. Let the breath settle. Bring to mind someone caught up in something that wasn't theirs: a stranger in the news, a person in the background of your own day, someone whose name you never learned. You don't need to fix anything. Just hold them in attention for a while, the way the story doesn't stop to. If you pray, you can hold them there. The bell holds the time.
Nishada, a woman of the forest people who slept in the house that night, with her five sons, and was never named.
Your line: a woman and five sons, unnamed. Today, learn the name of one person you usually pass without one. Day seven hundred thirty-seven.

738.title: the lac house
738.hook: Bhima carries his whole family through the dark, and a stranger at the river says the right words
738.carry: quiet help, hidden in plain sight
738.howItsDone: Vidura's counsel is read in its own right in Hindu tradition: the Vidura Niti, his advice to Dhritarashtra in the Udyoga Parva, is read by some as a book of practical wisdom.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the lac house burned, and the bodies of strangers were taken for the Pandavas' — a woman and five sons, unnamed. Did you learn someone's name? Day seven hundred thirty-eight.

Out of the tunnel, into a forest at night, with a town about to wake behind them. Kunti and her sons are worn out, and the dark is thick. So Bhima picks them up. All of them. The text sets it out: his mother up on his shoulders, the twins against his sides, Yudhishthira and Arjuna held by the hand. And he goes, pushing through the trees, carrying his whole family at once. The house is behind them. They still have to get away.
screen: `OUT OF THE TUNNEL.` → `BHIMA CARRIES THEM ALL.`

segments.voice: They reach the Ganga. And a man is waiting there, with a boat. He says Vidura sent him. But how can they know? Anyone could say that. So he gives the same kind of sign the digger gave: he speaks back words from the riddle Vidura used on the road, words only Yudhishthira understood. Only someone Vidura trusted could know them. Yudhishthira hears them, and the family gets into the boat. Look at what Vidura has done, start to finish. He couldn't stop the plot in the open. So he warned in a riddle, sent a miner to dig, and set a boat at the water's edge. None of it loud. Every piece hidden in plain sight. The boatman carries them across, sends them on with good wishes for the road, and goes back the way he came. What runs through this part of the lac house is trust. Bhima is trusted to carry everyone. The boatman is trusted on the strength of a few remembered words. And the whole family is trusting Vidura, who isn't even there. A shared secret becomes a kind of key. Some readers see Vidura in this story as the quiet conscience of the Kuru house: the one who can't change the king's mind, but keeps a door open anyway. And the Pandavas, dead as far as the world knows, step off the boat on the far bank as people no one is looking for.
screen: `A BOAT WAITING AT THE GANGA.` · `VIDURA'S WORDS, SPOKEN BACK.` · `QUIET HELP, HIDDEN IN PLAIN SIGHT.` · `NO ONE LOOKING FOR THEM.`

segments.voice: Settle, and let the breath find its pace. Let the chair or the floor take your whole weight, the way Kunti let Bhima carry her through the dark. Notice how much of yourself you can hand over to what's holding you. Then bring to mind one person whose word you'd take without asking for proof. What makes their word enough? Stay with that for a few breaths. If you pray, you can hold them in your prayer. The bell holds the time.
Nauka, the boat waiting at the Ganga, its boatman proved trustworthy by repeating Vidura's own hidden words.
Your line: quiet help, hidden in plain sight. Today, do one helpful thing quietly, and don't mention it to anyone. Day seven hundred thirty-eight.

739.title: the lac house
739.hook: the city mourns the living, and in the forest Bhima keeps watch
739.howItsDone: Offering water for the dead, called tarpana, is part of Hindu funeral and remembrance rites; in this story the offering is made for the Pandavas while they are still alive.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the lac house fell behind them: Bhima carrying everyone, and a boatman who knew Vidura's words — quiet help, hidden in plain sight. Did you help someone quietly? Day seven hundred thirty-nine.

In Hastinapura, the news arrives: the Pandavas are dead, burned at Varanavata with their mother. Dhritarashtra weeps, the text says, and orders the rites for the dead. Water is offered for them. The people mourn. And Vidura grieves only a little, because he knows. Far away, the five brothers and their mother are alive, and asleep on the ground. Today, the last of the lac house: two nights, and two kinds of grief.

In the forest, they've gone as far as they can. Kunti is exhausted and thirsty. Bhima goes to find water, and by the time he brings it back, they're all asleep, on the bare ground under a tree. So Bhima sits up, alone, and looks at them. The text gives him a lament here. In paraphrase: what could hurt more than this, my brothers sleeping on the earth, my mother lying in the open like this. He thinks of Duryodhana, and his anger rises. He could go back and end it, he says. But Yudhishthira isn't angry, and Bhima won't move without him. So he stays where he is, and keeps watch. Set the two scenes side by side. In the city, a king weeps for nephews his own son tried to kill. The text doesn't tell us how to weigh those tears. Vidura holds his secret and says little. And in the forest, the brother known for his strength, and for his anger, spends it sitting still. Bhima is the brother we first met shaking boys out of a tree. Here, at the end of the lac house, his strength takes another shape. He doesn't go back to fight. He stays awake so the others can rest. The house is ash. The family is homeless, mourned as dead, sleeping in the open. And one of them is watching over the rest.
screen: `ASLEEP ON THE BARE GROUND.` · `BHIMA'S LAMENT, AND HIS ANGER.` · `HE WON'T MOVE WITHOUT YUDHISHTHIRA.` · then, large: `STRENGTH THAT KEEPS WATCH.`

segments.voice: Let the breath slow. Bring to mind the people who'll be asleep tonight, under your roof, or in your city, or far away: people you care about. If you live alone, think of one person, wherever they are. See them resting. For a moment, you're the one awake, like Bhima under the tree. There's nothing you need to do for them. Just keep watch in your mind, breathing slowly, while they sleep. The bell holds the time.
Bhima, the brother known for strength and anger, who spends this night sitting still, keeping watch while his family sleeps.
Your line: strength that keeps watch. Today, if anger rises, see whether it can turn into watchfulness instead, just once. Day seven hundred thirty-nine.

740.title: Draupadi's swayamvara
740.hook: a daughter rises from a sacrificial fire, and a king announces she will choose
740.carry: a princess born from the fire
740.howItsDone: Draupadi is honored as a goddess in parts of South India: some villages in Tamil Nadu keep temples to Draupadi Amman and hold festivals in her name, some with firewalking.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the lac house ended: a city mourning the living, and Bhima keeping watch under a tree — strength that keeps watch. Did your anger find another shape? Day seven hundred forty.

A king has a fire lit because he wants a son. Drupada of Panchala has been humbled by Drona, and he wants someone who can answer that. Priests perform a great sacrifice. From the fire a young man rises, armed and shining: Dhrishtadyumna. And then, from the middle of the altar, a young woman. Dark, the text says, with eyes like lotus petals, and the scent of blue lotus around her. The sacrifice was for a son. The fire gives a daughter too. Today, a new stretch of the serial: Draupadi's swayamvara.
screen: `A FIRE FOR A SON.` → `A DAUGHTER FROM THE ALTAR.`

segments.voice: As she rises, the text says, a voice is heard from the sky. This dark girl, it says, will bring about the destruction of the warrior class. She's named Krishnaa, the dark one, and she's also called Draupadi, Drupada's daughter, and Panchali, the princess of Panchala. Now the Pandavas hear about her. They're still in hiding, living as brahmins in a town, and a traveling brahmin tells them the whole story: the fire, the brother and sister, and the swayamvara Drupada has announced. A swayamvara is a choosing. A princess's own choosing of a husband, with the suitors gathered in one place. In another story the Mahabharata tells, Nala and Damayanti's, the princess walks among her suitors and garlands the one she wants. Drupada's swayamvara will work differently, and tomorrow we'll see how. For now, look at who's standing in the doorway of the story. A woman born from a fire, with a prophecy spoken over her before she's said a word. A father with an old wound. And five brothers the world thinks are dead, listening to a traveler's news in a borrowed room. The text says Kunti sees her sons grow restless at the news, and she says it's time to move on, to Panchala. So they set out, still dressed as brahmins.
screen: `A VOICE FROM THE SKY.` · `KRISHNAA, DRAUPADI, PANCHALI.` · `A SWAYAMVARA: HER CHOOSING.` · `THE PANDAVAS SET OUT.`

segments.voice: Settle into the breath. A name comes before anyone can choose it, and other people's hopes come with it. Bring to mind one thing that was said about you before you were old enough to answer. Hold it lightly, like something set in your hand. Breathe with it, and let yourself be more than it. Draupadi had a prophecy spoken over her at birth. The story will still give her a voice of her own. The bell holds the time.
Draupadi's swayamvara. The choosing of a husband for the princess born from the fire: Krishnaa, Draupadi, Panchali.
Your line: a princess born from the fire. Today, when someone tells you who you are, take one breath before you agree. Day seven hundred forty.

741.title: Draupadi's swayamvara
741.hook: a bow almost no one can bend, and a mark beyond a device set high in the air
741.carry: the kings fall, one by one
741.howItsDone: The contest at Panchala, with the bow and the mark, is shown in Hindu painting, dance and storytelling; in some retellings the archer aims at a fish's eye seen reflected in water below.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Draupadi's swayamvara was announced: a princess born from the fire, and five brothers setting out for Panchala. Did you take a breath before agreeing? Day seven hundred forty-one.

The arena at Panchala is packed. Kings and princes have come from far and wide, dressed in their best, crowding the stands. Brahmins have come to watch. There's music, and the noise of a crowd that has waited for this. And somewhere among the brahmins sit five brothers in borrowed clothes, whom everyone here believes are dead. Then Draupadi enters, carrying a garland, and her brother Dhrishtadyumna rises to announce the terms. Today we hear what it takes to win, and who can't.
screen: `A PACKED ARENA.` → `FIVE BROTHERS IN DISGUISE.` → `THE TERMS.`

segments.voice: Here's the challenge, in paraphrase. This is the bow, and these are the arrows. Up high is a mark, and in front of it a device set in the air, with an opening in it. Whoever strings the bow and shoots through the opening to hit the mark, and is worthy in birth and form and strength, wins my sister. Now a detail the text gives us. Drupada had hoped, all along, to give his daughter to Arjuna. So he had this bow made so stiff that hardly anyone could string it. One by one, the kings try. And one by one, the bow beats them. Some can't bend it at all. Some get close, and the bow springs back and throws them to the ground, their crowns and ornaments scattered across the floor. Great names, humbled in front of everyone. So here's what makes this swayamvara strange. The word means the bride's own choosing. But her choice runs through a test her father set, a test shaped around one man he hoped would come. The text doesn't say what Draupadi made of it. It shows her standing with the garland while her brother reads out the terms, and the kings walking up to the bow. Some retellings picture the mark as a fish's eye, seen in a reflection. In this passage it's simply a mark, beyond a device, very high up.
screen: `THE TERMS: STRING, SHOOT, HIT.` · `A BOW MADE FOR ONE MAN.` · `THE KINGS FALL, ONE BY ONE.` · `A CHOOSING, ROUTED THROUGH A TEST.`

segments.voice: Let the breath settle. Bring to mind a test you once faced that seemed designed for someone else: a job, a team, a room you didn't quite fit. Notice where the memory sits in the body. Then, with each breath out, let a little of it go. You aren't in that arena now. Just breathe here, where nothing has to be won. The bell holds the time.
Draupadi's swayamvara. A bow almost no one could bend, a mark beyond a device set high in the air, and kings thrown to the floor.
Your line: the kings fall, one by one. Today, when you face a test, ask who designed it, and for whom. Day seven hundred forty-one.

742.title: Draupadi's swayamvara
742.hook: Karna strings the bow, and one sentence stops him
742.howItsDone: Karna's story is retold in Hindu storytelling, theater and dance, and in modern novels, some of which tell the whole Mahabharata from his side.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Draupadi's swayamvara: the stiff bow, the mark set high, and kings thrown to the floor — the kings fall, one by one. Did you ask who designed a test? Day seven hundred forty-two.

This week opened in the lac house. Since then: a tunnel dug in secret, a fire lit from inside, a family carried through the forest, a boat at the river, Bhima awake under a tree, a princess born from a fire, and a bow that throws kings to the floor. Now, as the kings give up, a man rises whom we've met before. Karna. Found in a basket on the river, raised by a charioteer, born with armor on his body. He walks to the bow.

In the version Ganguli translated, Karna lifts the bow and strings it. He fits the arrows. He's about to shoot. And Draupadi speaks, loudly, so the whole arena hears. In paraphrase: I will not choose a suta for my husband. A suta: a charioteer, a charioteer's son. Karna laughs, a bitter laugh, the text says. He glances up at the sun. And he puts the bow down. That's all. A few lines. And they land on everything we've heard about Karna these past weeks. The basket on the river. Adhiratha the charioteer and his wife Radha, who raised him. The name Radheya. Birth deciding who may compete. Readers hear this moment in different ways. Some hear Draupadi holding the contest to its own terms: her brother announced that birth would count. Some hear her guarding her father's hope for Arjuna. Some hear the old sting of birth used against a man who could clearly do the thing. And some hear all of these at once. The poem doesn't settle it. It moves on. But stay a moment with that glance at the sun. The sun, as we know and the arena doesn't, is Karna's father. He looks up to him in the moment he's turned away, without knowing who he's looking at. Karna and Draupadi will meet again in another hall, later in this serial. For now, the bow is back on the ground, and the arena is waiting for someone else.
